study.title: Psalms 117 - A universal call to praise
study.overview: This psalm, the shortest of the Psalter, concludes with an invitation to all the nations and peoples to praise the Lord. The motive of praise is not in human merits, but in the abundant goodness of God and in the permanent fidelity of his word. In its brevity, psalm unites universal reach and theological depth: the God of Israel is worthy of the worship of all peoples because their love and truth remain forever.

outline.title: Universal Call to Praise
outline.explanation: The first verse summons all nations and all the peoples to celebrate the Lord. The focus is not a restricted group, but the worship that reaches the whole of humanity. The psalm thus presents a broad vision of the people of God, in which the Gentiles are also called to render honor to the Lord.

outline.title: Reason for praise: eternal kindness and faithfulness
outline.explanation: The second verse explains why praise is due: the goodness of the LORD prevails over his people, and their faithfulness endures forever. The psalm ends with an exclamation of worship, showing that the proper response to divine grace is continuous praise.

study.context: The notes highlight that this is the shortest psalm. They also note that the New Testament quotes him as a testimony that the Gentile nations would glorify the God of Israel. The tradition commented on in the notes reads the psalm in Messianic key and linked to the expansion of the gospel, although this appears as theological interpretation and not as an explicit statement of the text itself.
study.theology: The psalm teaches that praise to God is born of who he is and what he does: his goodness is great and his faithfulness is lasting. There is here a universal scope of divine grace, for the call is not limited to Israel, but includes all nations. Theologically, the text points to the constancy of God: he is not only kind in a moment, but permanently faithful. In the notes, this is related to salvation in Christ and to the inclusion of the Gentiles, a reading that harmonizes with the apostolic use of psalm, but must be understood as the Christian interpretation of the text.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm summons all the peoples of the earth to praise the Lord because of his infallible love and his permanent fidelity; the comment also highlights that Paul quotes this verse as proof of the future worship of the Gentiles to the God of Israel.
The commentary sees in this psalm a strong content of the gospel and understands that the convocation to praise includes in a special way the Gentiles, for whom the psalm casts a favorable look.
The note states that God's merciful goodness is powerful and prevails over sin, Satan, death, and hell, and that the truth of the Lord unfailingly fulfills what he promises.

questions: How does the fact that the psalm call all nations to praise extends our vision of worship to God?
How do God's goodness and faithfulness sustain praise even in difficult times?
How can the Christian reading of this psalm strengthen the mission of the church among the peoples?
study.practice: Take this psalm as a short prayer for the day: recognize before God your goodness that reaches you and your faithfulness that does not fail. Then practice a praise that includes other people, especially those that you would not normally imagine as a recipient of God's grace. If this psalm speaks of the nations, it also corrects any form of faith closed in itself. Praise the LORD with simplicity, but with conviction, remembering that his truth remains forever.
study.uncertainty: The chapter is very brief and the notes provided are few; therefore, the historical context was limited to what appears explicitly in the comments. Readings about the Messiah, the gospel, and the inclusion of the Gentiles are interpretations of the commentators and the later biblical use, not direct affirmations of the text of the Psalm.
